cards.back: A worker that runs code. Every program starts with one, main, and threads you start run at the same time and share the same objects.
start() creates a new thread that runs run(). Calling run() directly runs the code on the current thread, so there is still only one thread.

cards.front: What does new Thread(...) do on its own?
cards.back: It only creates an object. Nothing runs until start(), and start() can be called once per thread.
To enter a synchronized block a thread must hold the object's lock; others wait at the door. The lock is released automatically on leaving, so only one thread is inside at a time.
Releases the lock and sleeps until notified; wait(ms) also wakes when the time is up. It must be called inside synchronized.
Wakes one waiting thread, which must pick the lock back up before it continues. It must be called inside synchronized.

cards.front: Calling wait() or notify() without the lock
cards.back: Java throws IllegalMonitorStateException. Both must be called while holding the object's lock.

cards.front: Why re-check after waking from wait()?
cards.back: Waking means 'something happened', not 'your condition is true'. Loop back and check the condition again, for example whether the earliest alarm is actually due.
sleep() keeps the lock, cannot be woken by notify() and needs no synchronized. wait() releases the lock and can be woken early.
A background thread that the JVM does not wait for before exiting. setDaemon(true) must be called before start().

cards.front: What to use in real code for an alarm scheduler
cards.back: ScheduledExecutorService. Interviewers often ask for the hand-built version, so mention it at the end.

quiz.q: The alarm worker calls Thread.sleep(5000) inside synchronized. What happens when schedule(2000) is called?
choices: It blocks until the sleep ends, so the 2 s alarm rings late
It runs in parallel and the alarm rings on time
quiz.why: sleep() keeps the lock, so schedule() cannot get in.

quiz.q: Code calls t.run() instead of t.start() on a thread that loops forever. What happens?
choices: The caller runs the loop itself and gets stuck
A new thread runs the loop
The loop runs once and returns
quiz.why: run() does not create a new thread.

quiz.q: The alarm worker loops forever and is not a daemon. What happens when main finishes?
quiz.why: Java waits for all normal threads before exiting.

quiz.q: schedule() adds an alarm but forgets to call notify(). What goes wrong?
choices: The waiting worker may never wake to see the new alarm
quiz.why: A thread in wait() without a timeout sleeps until notified.

choices: Any time while the thread is alive
quiz.why: Calling it after the thread has started is a classic mistake.

quiz.q: Why does a synchronized block protect a shared PriorityQueue?
choices: Only one thread can be inside at a time, so changes take turns
It copies the queue for each thread
It runs the block on the main thread
quiz.why: Two threads changing the queue at the same moment can break it.
